# The exact-kernel MeshTransformer {#sec-mt1}

The exact-kernel MeshTransformer (MT1 from here on) is a boundary-to-field
operator learner that puts the singular part of potential theory into the
network as closed-form panel integrals and learns only the smooth
coefficients that multiply them. One layer of signed, quadrature-weighted
attention over the boundary cells plays the role of the boundary solve; a
decoder then evaluates two exact free-space kernels, the double-layer and
the single-layer Laplace potentials, integrated exactly over every boundary
cell, with coefficients conditioned on the encoded boundary. Everything the
network computes is an invariant scalar or a polar vector, positions are
nondimensionalized by a gauge derived from the geometry itself, and the
boundary data enters through a stream whose algebraic law (linear,
degree-two, degree-one, or merely zero-preserving) is declared per problem.
The result is a model of about 82k parameters whose contracts, similarity
equivariance, drive linearity when declared, parity typing, and query
independence, hold for any weights and are asserted as tests.

This design is what the controlled suites of Part III measure
(@sec-linear-suites, @sec-nonlinear-suites). It generalizes across
boundary-condition frequency content on linear problems where soft-slice
and moment decoders do not, and it extrapolates amplitude exactly under a
declared linearity contract. It also stops where its prior stops: the
potential-flow structure it encodes is not a usable prior for separated 3D
aerodynamics, and on the DrivAerML interior task it is 8x behind
GeoTransolver-volume, a comparison that is not resource-matched:
GeoTransolver-volume has 9.0M parameters and MT1's parameter count on that
task was not recorded (@sec-industrial-mt1, @sec-interior). MeshTransformer2 (@sec-mt2) is the
architecture that keeps MT1's equivariance and drops its kernel dictionary;
the last section of this chapter states the relation.

## The architecture {#sec-architecture}

MT1 computes one thing: given the boundary of a domain, its shape, the
type of boundary condition on each patch, and the boundary values, predict
a physical field at any set of points (@sec-problem states the problem
class). Encoding runs once per boundary; decoding runs for any number of
query points afterwards and reuses the encoding.

The input is a boundary mesh: surface cells (line segments in 2D,
triangles in 3D), each carrying its centroid, its measure (length or
area), its outward normal, a one-hot label naming the boundary patch it
belongs to, and whatever fields are declared on that patch. Domain-level
scalars (a material parameter, a screening constant) and vectors (a
freestream direction) arrive as global data. Every declared field has one
of two *roles*: **operator** fields describe the problem (geometry,
material, PDE coefficients) and may be used nonlinearly; **drive** fields
are the data the solution depends on (boundary values, fluxes, a far-field
velocity), and zero drive must produce zero output. The output is a typed
prediction at each query point, invariant scalars and polar vectors by
declared rank, written to the query mesh. Nothing about the interior is
supplied: no interior mesh, no initial guess, no source term.

### The forward pass {#sec-forward-pass}

Five stages, in words. First, **nondimensionalize**: subtract the
measure-weighted centre of the boundary and divide every length by a
reference length derived from the boundary itself (its measure-weighted
RMS radius); downstream, nothing ever sees an absolute position or size.
Second, **lift**: each cell's normalized position, normal, patch label,
and operator fields become a small set of scalar channels and vector
channels, and a shared pointwise typed block enriches them without any
interaction. Third, **boundary self-attention**: one layer in which every
cell reads a signed, measure-weighted combination of every other cell's
state, the global coupling of an elliptic boundary-value problem. Fourth,
**drive read-in**: the boundary and global drive fields are lifted by a
map that is linear in the drive at fixed operator state, then propagated
boundary-to-boundary by field blocks of the declared algebraic class.
Fifth, **kernel decode**: for each query point the two exact singular
kernels are integrated in closed form over every cell and summed with
coefficients read from the encoded boundary, followed by a bias-free typed
output projection.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mt1-forward
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The MT1 forward pass. Grey boxes are data (the input mesh, the query
#|   points, the cached encoding, and the output prediction); purple boxes
#|   are computation. Encode (left of the cache) runs once per
#|   boundary in time linear in the number of cells; decode runs per query
#|   batch at a cost proportional to (queries x cells) and never lets query
#|   points interact. How to read this: the diagram shows information flow,
#|   not tensor shapes or parameter counts; the reference configuration

box(10.2, 0.35, 3.6, H, "typed prediction at queries\nscalars, polar vectors", "data")

```

The gauge step is the one place where a convention could enter, so it is
worth writing down. With cell centroids $y_j$ and effective cell measures
$w_j$ (geometric measure times any declared sampling weight), the code
(`gauge.measure_weighted_rms_radius`, called from
`MeshTransformer.encode` when `reference_length_key` is `None`) forms

| symbol | meaning | code |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ | measure-weighted boundary centre | `center` in `encode` |
| $L$ | reference length: measure-weighted RMS radius about $c$ | `measure_weighted_rms_radius` |
| $z_j,\ \zeta_i$ | normalized source centroid, normalized query point | `source_points`, query points / `L` |
| $\omega_j$ | normalized cell measure $w_j / L^{D-1}$ | `cell_measures(source_mesh)` |

$$
c=\frac{\sum_j w_j\,y_j}{\sum_j w_j},\qquad
L=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_j w_j\,\lVert y_j-c\rVert^2}{\sum_j w_j}},\qquad
z_j=\frac{y_j-c}{L},\quad \zeta_i=\frac{x_i-c}{L}.
$$

$L$ is positively homogeneous of degree one in the geometry: scale the
boundary by $s$ and $L$ scales by exactly $s$, so the normalized
coordinates are unchanged. Scale equivariance therefore does not depend on
a caller supplying a consistent length. A `reference_length_key` override
exists for canonically dimensioned problems (an aerodynamic chord); it is
discussed with its cost in @sec-intrinsic-gauge.

### Typed channels and the mirror test {#sec-typed-channels}

Every latent quantity in MT1 is one of two types, and the distinction is
physical. An **invariant scalar** is a number every observer agrees on
under rotation or reflection: a distance, a dot product, a temperature. A
**polar vector** is an ordinary arrow, a displacement, a velocity, a
surface normal: rotate the scene and it rotates with it. The type MT1
deliberately excludes is exposed by the mirror test. Hold a spinning wheel
before a mirror: its velocity arrows reflect like ordinary arrows, but its
spin axis does not; the image spins the other way, so the reflected axis
points where "reflect like an arrow" says it should not. Such quantities,
cross products, curls, rotation axes, are **axial vectors**; the analogous
sign-flipping number (a signed area or volume) is a **pseudoscalar**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mirror
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The mirror test. Left: a polar vector (velocity) reflects like an
#|   ordinary arrow. Right: an axial vector (the wheel's spin axis) comes back
#|   flipped relative to naive reflection because the mirror image spins the
#|   other way. MT1 carries scalars and polar vectors only; axial quantities
#|   are rejected at construction time. How to read this: a schematic of
#|   transformation laws, not a measurement. Not computed from an artifact.
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INK, INK2, PURPLE, RED = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#7b4fb3", "#e34948"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.0))
for ax, title, flipped in ((axes[0], "polar vector (velocity)", False),
                           (axes[1], "axial vector (spin axis)", True)):
    ax.plot([0, 0], [-1.05, 1.15], color=INK, lw=2.5)
    ax.text(0, 1.22, "mirror", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=INK)
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((-1.0, 0.0), 0.52, fill=False, color=INK2, lw=1.4))
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((1.0, 0.0), 0.52, fill=False, color=INK2, lw=1.4, ls="--"))
    if not flipped:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.35, 0.0), xytext=(-1.0, 0.0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=PURPLE, lw=2.4))
        ax.annotate("", xy=(0.35, 0.0), xytext=(1.0, 0.0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=PURPLE, lw=2.4, ls="--"))
    else:
        for cx, up, ls in ((-1.0, True, "-"), (1.0, False, "--")):
            dy = 0.62 if up else -0.62
            ax.annotate("", xy=(cx, dy), xytext=(cx, 0.0),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=RED, lw=2.4, ls=ls))
            theta = np.linspace(0.35 * np.pi, 1.15 * np.pi, 40)
            direction = 1.0 if up else -1.0
            ax.plot(cx + 0.40 * np.cos(direction * theta), 0.40 * np.sin(direction * theta),
                    color=INK2, lw=1.1)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.9, 1.9); ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.5)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
```

The problem class has no handedness: reflect a Laplace problem and its
solution reflects. Scalars and polar vectors are two irreducible
representations of the rotation-reflection group $O(D)$, and MT1 uses
exactly these two. `ScalarVectorState` holds scalar channels of shape
$(N, C_s)$ and vector channels of shape $(N, C_v, D)$; `TypedProjection`
implements the only allowed combinations: any function of scalars is a
scalar, dot products of vectors are scalars (this is how vector
information reaches scalar channels), and new vectors are made only as
scalar-weighted sums of existing vectors, never from raw components. A
layer that would produce anything else fails at construction. Because no
learned map ever sees a Cartesian component, equivariance holds to
floating point for any weights.

One typed extension exists for 2D problems whose target is parity-odd (a
circulation): pseudoscalar channels (`0o`) with the wedge product as a
typed operation. The reference configuration does not use them; the 3D
analogue (axial vectors) is excluded.

### Attention as a boundary solve {#sec-attention-role}

Elliptic boundary-value problems are global: the solution at one end of
the domain depends on data at the other. Boundary-integral methods make
this explicit by solving a dense linear system over all boundary
elements. MT1's boundary self-attention is the learned analogue, and it
departs from textbook attention in three ways, each forced by the
physics: the pair weights are **signed** (no softmax; boundary-integral
kernels change sign), sources contribute in proportion to their **measure**
(so refinement converges rather than double-counting), and the coupling is
**separable**, factored through a small set of global moments so the encode
cost is linear in the cell count. How much attention the physics needs is
an empirical question with a measured answer on the controlled suites: one
layer, one full-width head (@sec-linear-suites). All-Dirichlet problems
nearly work with none; mixed Dirichlet/Neumann problems need one.

### The decoder: exact kernels, learned coefficients {#sec-decoder-role}

The decoder asks: given the encoded boundary, what is the field at $x$?
Any solution of a homogeneous elliptic problem is a boundary integral of
known singular kernels against unknown boundary densities (the Green
representation). MT1's decoder mirrors this: for each query and each
boundary cell it evaluates the free-space double-layer and single-layer
Laplace kernels *integrated exactly over the cell*, closed forms rather
than point samples, and multiplies them by smooth coefficients produced
from the encoded boundary state. The learning is in the coefficients; the
singular structure is exact.

Why closed forms matter is easiest to see one panel at a time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-panel-integral
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Why the decoder integrates rather than samples. For a query point
#|   approaching the midpoint of a unit 2D panel, the exact cell integral of
#|   the double-layer kernel (the signed subtended angle over 2 pi, as in
#|   kernel_decoder.exact_double_layer_member) saturates at 1/2, while the
#|   midpoint-quadrature estimate (length x kernel value at the centroid)
#|   diverges like 1/distance. A learned coefficient cannot repair a factor
#|   that blows up under infinitesimal displacement. How to read this: the
#|   grey curve is a query at 0.75 panel-lengths off the panel's span, where
#|   both agree; the figure shows the near-field failure of point sampling,
#|   not a trained model. Computed from the closed form; not from an artifact.
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INK2, PURPLE, MUTED, GRID = "#52514e", "#7b4fb3", "#898781", "#e1e0d9"
h = 1.0
d = np.logspace(-3, 0.5, 200)

def exact(x0, d):
    # signed subtended angle of the panel [-h/2, h/2] x {0} seen from (x0, d), over 2 pi
    return (np.arctan2(d, x0 - h / 2) - np.arctan2(d, x0 + h / 2)) / (2 * np.pi)

def midpoint(x0, d):
    # length x (n . r) / (2 pi |r|^2) with n = (0, 1), r = (x0, d)
    return h * d / (2 * np.pi * (x0**2 + d**2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
ax.plot(d, exact(0.0, d), color=PURPLE, lw=2.2, label="exact panel integral (query over panel centre)")
ax.plot(d, midpoint(0.0, d), color=PURPLE, lw=1.6, ls="--", label="midpoint quadrature (same query)")
ax.plot(d, exact(0.75 * h, d), color=MUTED, lw=1.6, label="exact, query 0.75 h off the span")
ax.plot(d, midpoint(0.75 * h, d), color=MUTED, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="midpoint, query 0.75 h off the span")
ax.axhline(0.5, color=INK2, lw=0.9, ls=":")
ax.text(1.15e-3, 0.62, "1/2: the one-sided limit on the panel", fontsize=8, color=INK2, va="bottom")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("distance from panel [panel lengths]")
ax.set_ylabel("double-layer cell integral [dimensionless]")
ax.set_ylim(1e-3, 3e2)
import numpy as _np
for line in ax.get_lines():
    if line.get_label().startswith("_"):
        continue
    xd, yd = _np.asarray(line.get_xdata()), _np.asarray(line.get_ydata())
    k = int(_np.argmin(_np.abs(_np.log(xd) - _np.log(0.02))))  # label where the four curves are well separated
    below = line.get_label().startswith("exact panel integral")
    ax.annotate(line.get_label(), (xd[k], yd[k]), xytext=(8, -6 if below else 5), textcoords="offset points",
                color=line.get_color(), fontsize=8, ha="left", va="top" if below else "bottom",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
plt.tight_layout()
```

Two exact members make up the dictionary in the reference configuration.
The **double-layer member** (`exact_double_layer_member`) is the exact
cell integral of $\partial_{n_y} G$: in 2D the signed subtended angle of
the segment, with the orientation factor $\sigma = n\times\tau$ that makes
the value odd in the normal as the double layer requires; in 3D the
van Oosterom–Strackee signed solid angle of the triangle, whose entries at
an interior point of a closed boundary sum to exactly $-1$. The
**single-layer member** (`exact_single_layer_member`) is the exact cell
integral of $G$ itself: the Hess–Smith constant-strength source-panel
closed form in 2D and a per-edge $\operatorname{asinh}$ form plus solid
angle in 3D. It is even in the normal and carries the net flux that a pure
double-layer representation cannot (through the handles of a multiply
connected domain, for instance). Both are validated against brute-force
quadrature to about $10^{-14}$. Neither has a learned parameter of its
own; the learning is in the coefficient that multiplies each member.

A declared **boundary-trace mode** (`trace_of`) extends the decoder to
boundary-to-boundary targets such as surface pressure. A layer potential
is discontinuous across its own layer (the double layer's exterior and
interior traces differ from the principal value by $\pm 1/2$), so a query
placed on its own source panel receives whichever branch floating point
selects, and no coefficient can repair a term that flips sign under
infinitesimal displacement. The mode declares that the query mesh is the
named boundary's cell centroids, index-aligned, and licenses exactly two
changes: own-panel double-layer entries take the exterior one-sided
limit, exactly $+1/2$ in 2D and 3D (`exterior_trace_self_entries`; the
single layer is continuous and needs none), and each query reads its own
cell's encoded state. Every contract survives; query independence holds
given the declared identity map.

Two further knobs are opt-in and off in the reference configuration: a
declared auxiliary length scale (`kernel_auxiliary_scale_key`), which
rescales the pair invariants to a second physical scale such as a
boundary layer for the learned smooth members only, and a monopole-free
deflation of the single-layer member for exterior fields with zero net
flux, which is not licensed where net flux is the physics.

## The mathematics {#sec-mesh-attention}

This section is keyed to `physicsnemo/experimental/nn/mesh_attention/`
(`attention.py`, `block.py`, `model.py`, `kernel_decoder.py`, `gauge.py`).
The stack generalizes GLOBE (arXiv 2511.15856), keeping its invariant-only
learned maps, all-to-all quadrature-weighted boundary coupling, and
nondimensionalization, and replacing its bespoke kernel MLPs with
attention blocks, residual streams, and typed projections.

### Signed moment attention

`MeshAttention` is a finite-rank separable signed integral operator.
Typed projections of the operator state give, per head $h$, scalar and
vector query and key features, and the pair coefficient is a sum of scalar
products and vector dot products.

| symbol | meaning | code |
|---|---|---|
| $q^0_{ihr}, k^0_{jhr}$ | scalar query/key features, rank index $r\le R_0$ | `TypedQK`, `scalar_rank` |
| $q^1_{ihr}, k^1_{jhr}\in\mathbb R^D$ | vector query/key features, $r\le R_1$ | `vector_rank` |
| $a_{ijh}$ | signed pair coefficient, receiver $i$, source $j$, head $h$ | inside `MeshAttention.forward` |
| $\omega_j$ | normalized cell measure | `cell_measures(source_mesh)` |
| $v_{jhf}$ | typed value channel $f$ (scalar or vector) | `TypedValues` |
| $M$ | source moments, four typed blocks | `AttentionMoments`, `integrate_moment` |

$$
a_{ijh}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{R_0+DR_1}}\Bigl(\sum_{r\le R_0} q^0_{ihr}k^0_{jhr}
+\sum_{r\le R_1} q^1_{ihr}\!\cdot\!k^1_{jhr}\Bigr),
\qquad
o_{ihf}=\sum_j \omega_j\,a_{ijh}\,v_{jhf}.
$$

There is no softmax (kernels are signed), no distance envelope or cutoff
(elliptic problems are global), and no normalization (it would break drive
linearity). Because $a_{ijh}$ is bilinear in query and key features, the
all-pairs sum reassociates exactly into source moments built once,
$M^{00}_{hrf}=\sum_j\omega_j k^0_{jhr}v^0_{jhf}$ and its three typed
siblings, and contracted at each receiver; encode is linear in the cell
count and the rearrangement is exact (a dense `forward_reference` backs
value- and gradient-equality tests). The price is rank: per head the pair
kernel has rank at most $R_0+DR_1$, so one layer cannot represent an
arbitrary pair function, and in particular not a singular Green kernel.
Heads and ranks are capacity knobs, not physics.

### From the angular ceiling to the kernel decoder {#sec-kernel-decoder}

The rank limit becomes a theorem at the query. At an ordinary interior
query the only query-side vector is the normalized position $\zeta$, so a
separable moment decoder in linear mode with scalar output can only
produce $u(\zeta)=c(|\zeta|^2)+b(|\zeta|^2)\cdot\zeta+\zeta^{\mathsf T}A(|\zeta|^2)\zeta$:
on any circle about the origin the angular content is limited to Fourier
orders $m\le 2$, whatever the width, depth, or rank. A paired random-weight
ring test (`test_kernel_decoder.py`) asserts the moment decoder's $m\ge 3$
content is below $2\times10^{-11}$ and the kernel decoder's above
$10^{-6}$. The fix changes what the decoder *is*: `query_decoder="kernel"`
replaces the moment contraction with a dense, operator-conditioned
pair-kernel dictionary.

| symbol | meaning | code |
|---|---|---|
| $\varphi_m(\zeta, z_j)$ | dictionary member $m$: exact cell integral of a kernel over cell $j$ | `exact_double_layer_member`, `exact_single_layer_member` |
| $C_{mh}(\mathrm{op}_j)$ | member coefficient, a linear map of source $j$'s operator invariants | `coefficient_map` |
| $V_{jhf}$ | bias-free typed value of the drive state at source $j$ | `value_projection` |
| $u_{hf}(\zeta)$ | decoded field at the query, head $h$, channel $f$ | message assembled in `KernelBasisCrossDecoder.forward` |

$$
u_{hf}(\zeta)=\sum_j \kappa_h(\zeta, z_j)\,V_{jhf},\qquad
\kappa_h(\zeta, z_j)=\sum_m C_{mh}(\mathrm{op}_j)\,\varphi_m(\zeta, z_j).
$$

The operator invariants feeding $C_{mh}$ are the source's operator scalars
plus the Gram invariants of its operator vectors; in the linear class the
coefficients and pair features never read the drive, so the message is
exactly linear in the drive at fixed geometry. All pair features are joint
$O(D)$ invariants of $\{\zeta - z_j,\ n_j,\ \text{source-state vectors}\}$
(`PairInvariantFeatures`: $\lVert r\rVert^2$, $n\cdot r$, $v_c\cdot r$),
so no absolute position or orientation enters. The two linearity classes
are separate Python classes (`LinearKernelBasisCrossDecoder`,
`NonlinearZeroKernelBasisCrossDecoder`), so a bias added to one cannot
silently invalidate the other's proof. On the frozen 2D Laplace reference
bank (relative L2, 3-seed means, 3,000 updates) the kernel decoder with
its full dictionary of singular, polynomial, and eight MLP members
(110,561 parameters) cuts the in-distribution error of the moment decoder
at the same encoder capacity (135,945 parameters) by 11.3x, 0.4503 to
0.0399; the two-member dictionary of the reference configuration is priced
against this full dictionary in @sec-dictionary-ablation, and
@tbl-mt1-laplace-configs maps every 2D Laplace figure quoted in this
chapter to its configuration.

### Two streams {#sec-stream-factorization}

Input fields flow through two streams that are different Python classes.
The **operator stream** (`MeshOperatorBlock`: typed RMS norm, moment
attention, equivariant feed-forward, LayerScale residuals) may use biases
and nonlinearities because it describes the operator, not the solution
amplitude. The **drive stream** carries the data the solution depends on,
and its class is declared per problem by `field_mode`:

| mode | class | law of the drive-to-output map at fixed geometry |
|---|---|---|
| `linear` | `LinearMeshFieldBlock` | exactly linear: zero drive gives zero, superposition holds to floating point |
| `quadratic` | `QuadraticFieldReadIn` | exact polynomial of degree at most 2: the linear path plus one bilinear typed composition at the query read-in |
| `homogeneous` | `HomogeneousFieldReadIn` | degree one without additivity: $f(F)=\lVert F\rVert\,g(F/\lVert F\rVert)$ with $g$ a biased nonlinear typed map |
| `zero_preserving_nonlinear` | `NonlinearZeroMeshFieldBlock` | zero drive gives zero; keys and values read the drive through multiplicative updates; degree unconstrained |

In `linear` mode, queries and keys read only the operator state, values
are bias-free and linear in the drive, and the pointwise maps are
`GeometryConditionedLinear`: geometry may convert types (field vector dot
geometry vector to scalar; field scalar times geometry vector to vector;
a dyad branch for anisotropic maps like $(v\cdot n)n$) while staying
exactly linear in the field. The `quadratic` composition sits at the
read-in rather than in a stackable block because residual bilinear
updates would compose to degree $2^k$. The `homogeneous` mode fits
targets that depend nonlinearly on the drive's *shape* but linearly on
its *amplitude* (nondimensional surface loads under a unit freestream)
and is wrong where amplitude nonlinearity is the physics. The nonlinear
mode's implicit drive degree, measured at about 21 on the synthetic
suites, is what the declared-degree modes exist to forbid
(@sec-nonlinear-fragility).

The factorization was priced against a single-stream control that
re-declares the drive as operator features, matched in parameters within
0.03%, on 2D Laplace in linear mode (3-seed means, relative L2 on the
frozen reference bank, both arms in the benchmark-capacity sibling
configuration of @sec-reference-config: four heads, two layers, two exact
members, 104,537 parameters). The two-stream model wins in-distribution,
0.0485 against the single-stream control's 0.0606, and is the only arm
with exact contracts: its zero-drive
output is exactly zero and its superposition violation is $10^{-7}$, where
the control *learns* approximate linearity and plateaus at 0.038 and
0.042, five decades above the structural contract. The factorization did
not improve frequency extrapolation (0.211 against the control's 0.179);
spectral generalization lives in the dictionary and its conditioning
(@sec-dictionary-ablation), not in the linearity contract. One caveat
travels with zero preservation: it is correct physics only when the
homogeneous problem has the zero solution. On the Liouville equation zero
Dirichlet data has the interior solution $\log 4$, so the contract pins
the wrong value exactly. A contract can be exactly enforced and exactly
wrong; each declaration needs a per-problem correctness
check.^[`results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json`, key
`iteration_26_stream_factorization` (the Laplace arms under `laplace_3seed`,
the Liouville arms under `liouville_3seed`).]

### The intrinsic similarity gauge {#sec-intrinsic-gauge}

The reference length is the last externally trusted input, so MT1 derives
it from the geometry by default (@sec-forward-pass). The measured
consequences on the frozen 2D Laplace reference bank (3-seed means,
relative L2, the benchmark-capacity sibling with the double-layer member
only, 104,261 parameters): the intrinsic gauge is accuracy-neutral against
an explicit per-case key (in-distribution 0.0372 with the intrinsic gauge
against 0.0375 with the explicit key; frequency split likewise), trained
models are similarity-covariant to $3\times10^{-7}$ under rotations,
reflections, translations, and rescalings by 0.2x to 5x, and a 3x
corruption of the supplied length at evaluation time degrades the
explicit-key model 4.64x while the intrinsic model is bitwise unchanged
because the input it would have trusted no longer
exists.^[`results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json`, key
`iteration_24_intrinsic_gauge`.]

The override is a loaded gun. A constant with units of length encodes one
dataset's absolute size and does not transform with the geometry, so for
any geometry from a different family the scale contract provides no
protection. The rule: if the gauge is overridden, override it with a
similarity-covariant functional of the input geometry (a per-case chord or
diameter), never with a number in a config file. Separately, geometric
scale is a symmetry of the *architecture*, not necessarily of the
*problem*: rescaling lengths at fixed dimensional viscosity changes the
Reynolds number, so the contract applies only when the complete
nondimensional problem transforms consistently.

### Cost and scale {#sec-scale}

Encode is linear in the number of boundary cells because attention is
separable. Decode is dense: $O(N_q N_s)$ work for $N_q$ queries and $N_s$
cells, chunked over queries so the forward peak is one chunk. During
training autograd retains every chunk's pair activations, so the
retained memory is the full $O(N_q N_s)$; the `kernel_checkpoint_query_chunks`
knob recomputes each chunk in the backward pass instead, and because the
decoder is RNG-free and shape-deterministic the recomputation is bitwise,
changing what is stored and nothing else, at the price of one extra
decode forward per backward. A Barnes–Hut backend exists as a separate
approximate numerical backend converging to the dense oracle; the
contracts stated in this chapter are those of the exact dense path.

## Where the kernel came from {#sec-learned-bie}

The dictionary is not a guess; it is the survivor of a falsification
ladder on 2D Laplace with exact conformal-map labels (relative L2 on the
frozen 64-case reference bank, 3 seeds; none of the models in this ladder
is MT1, so the errors below are not entries of @tbl-mt1-laplace-configs
and differ from it in parameter count and training length as stated per
model). A free-form learned pair kernel of 19,008
parameters reaches 0.107 in-distribution but 0.642 on unseen boundary
frequencies after 1,000 updates: a value interpolator with no operator
fidelity. Wrapping it in a learned second-kind solve does not help; soft
PDE or trace penalties move their own diagnostic and nothing else; an
exactly harmonic basis under midpoint quadrature loses badly, because
singular terms cannot mollify near-panel quadrature error. Only the
combination works: an exactly harmonic basis containing the true kernel,
exact panel quadrature, and a learned drive-linear density solve. A
3-parameter model of this form reaches 0.0347 in-distribution and 0.0664
on unseen frequencies after 3,000 updates, and its learned singular
coefficient lands within 0.8% of the classical $-1/2\pi$ on every seed,
from random initialization, on interior supervision
alone.^[`results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json`: the pair-kernel control
under `comparisons_same_bank`, the ladder under `hypothesis_chain`, the
3-parameter model under `iteration_4_pruning`
(`confirmation_3seed_reference_bank`). The full-length ladder with its
per-ingredient table is in @sec-linear-suites.]

The parametric study on screened Laplace disks adds the second rule:
known operator dependence belongs in a correctly normalized
fundamental-solution kernel, while learned coefficient conditioning
interpolates within its parameter range and cannot be assumed to
extrapolate beyond it. Together these fix MT1's division of labour: the
dictionary carries the singularity, the conditioning carries the
smoothness. Under the program's scope the governing equations are not
given, so the Laplace kernels are a prior rather than a specification;
how far that prior reaches is what the rest of the book measures.

## Declared contracts {#sec-mt1-contracts}

Each contract is a structural property that holds for any weights, and
each is asserted as a test rather than averaged into a score.

| contract | mechanism | test |
|---|---|---|
| similarity equivariance (rotation, reflection, translation, scale) | typed channels; intrinsic gauge | paired transformed cases agree to $128\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{fp32}}$; measured $\sim 3\times10^{-7}$ on trained models |
| zero drive gives zero output | bias-free drive path in every field mode | zero-drive evaluation, every mode |
| drive linearity, when declared | `linear` mode: keys read operator state only, values bias-free | two-drive superposition to $\sim10^{-7}$ |
| declared drive degree | `quadratic` / `homogeneous` read-ins | drive-scaling probe fits the declared polynomial to fp64 roundoff |
| parity typing | scalars and polar vectors only; opt-in `0o` in 2D | construction-time rejection; reflection tests |
| query independence | decode reads only the cached encoding and the query's own position | bitwise row-stability across query subsets and orderings |
| exact singular quadrature | closed-form panel integrals | agreement with brute-force quadrature to $\sim10^{-14}$ |

## The reference configuration {#sec-reference-config}

The configuration the controlled-suite evidence selects (@sec-linear-suites,
@sec-dictionary-ablation) is the smallest that matches everything
measured. Parameter counts are for the 2D Laplace scalar-output problem.

| piece | setting |
|---|---|
| typed lift | scalar/vector channels 32/8 (operator), 48/12 (drive) |
| boundary self-attention | 1 layer, 1 full-width head, separable ranks 48 (scalar) + 16 (vector) |
| drive read-in | zero-preserving; `linear` on linear problems, `quadratic` or `homogeneous` on known-degree targets, `zero_preserving_nonlinear` otherwise |
| decoder dictionary | 2 exact members (double layer + single layer), no polynomial or MLP members |
| total parameters | 81,547 |

A sibling configuration at the frozen benchmark capacity, 4 heads with
separable ranks 12/4, two encoder layers, the same two exact members,
104,537 parameters, is used wherever an arm must remain comparable with
every archived arm on the controlled suites; the two differ in attention
bookkeeping, not in the decoder. Because this chapter quotes 2D Laplace
in-distribution errors for several such configurations, the table below
maps each figure to the configuration that produced it; the suite results
themselves live in @sec-linear-suites. All rows are relative L2 on the
frozen 64-case 2D Laplace reference bank, 3-seed means, 3,000 updates,
linear drive mode, intrinsic gauge unless stated.

| configuration | parameters | 2D Laplace in-distribution rel-L2 | where in this chapter |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| reference configuration: 1 head (ranks 48/16), 1 layer, two exact members | 81,547 | not measured on this bank; selected on the cross-suite evidence of @sec-linear-suites | this section |

| benchmark-capacity sibling: 4 heads (ranks 12/4), two layers, two exact members | 104,537 | 0.0485 | @sec-stream-factorization |

by configuration. The learned boundary-integral ladder of
@sec-learned-bie (0.107 and 0.0347) is excluded because those models are
not MT1. `results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json`, keys
`iteration_31_heads_vs_rank` (rows 2–3), `iteration_11_dictionary_ablation_2d`

Two caveats travel with the reference row. The vector channels are prunable on easy 2D geometry but essential
in 3D and on parametric problems. The single-layer member is decisively
necessary on multiply connected and deeply cavitated geometry and costs
some frequency extrapolation on very easy geometry, because its
coefficient is freely fit rather than determined by a boundary system.
Industrial variants (@sec-industrial-mt1) are wider but keep this
structure.

## What the architecture excludes {#sec-mt1-exclusions}

Each exclusion is a falsifiable statement with a test attached.

| never | because | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| read an absolute coordinate, orientation, or index | equivariance for any weights | no positional encodings, Fourier features, PCA frames, or vertex embeddings anywhere |
| mix types outside the allowed products | no symmetry leaks, no hidden axial quantities | construction-time rejection |
| couple query points to each other | streaming evaluation; predictions independent of the query set | no interior mesh, graph, or neighbourhood |
| respond to zero drive | a homogeneous problem with no data has the zero solution | exact in every field mode (and exactly wrong where that premise fails, as on Liouville) |
| break superposition in `linear` mode | when the problem is linear its law should be structural | one class per declared law |
| point-sample a singular kernel | near-boundary accuracy | closed-form members only |
| use a distance cutoff, neighbourhood, or tree in the exact path | elliptic problems are global | dense decode, with its cost stated in @sec-scale |

Also excluded, by ablation rather than principle: polynomial and MLP
smooth members on linear problems (they trade structure for interpolation
and damage frequency extrapolation; @sec-dictionary-ablation), extra
attention layers, and multiple heads at fixed score capacity.

## What this design buys, and where it stops {#sec-mt1-scope}

On controlled linear problems the exact kernels buy exactly what the
Green representation promises. On the 2D Laplace, screened, and mixed
boundary-condition families with exact labels, the exact-kernel decoder
reaches relative L2 0.070 on the held-out frequency band where soft-slice
and moment-decoder arms sit at about 1.0, meaning no response at all
(@sec-linear-suites). Under a declared linearity contract it extrapolates
amplitude exactly, and leaving linearity undeclared costs 4.5x to 12x on
the same problems. Its two exact members, with no learned parameters of
their own, match a dictionary of eight learned kernel members
(@sec-dictionary-ablation). On the nonlinear suites the implicit drive
degree of the unconstrained mode is diagnosed and then declared away
(@sec-nonlinear-suites, @sec-nonlinear-fragility).

The line stops where the prior stops. On separated 3D aerodynamics the
potential-flow structure MT1 encodes is not a usable prior: the
potential-flow oracle reaches relative L2 4.8 where predicting each case's
mean pressure reaches 0.77, so no coefficient conditioning of these
kernels can recover the field (@sec-industrial-mt1). On DrivAerML surface
targets the boundary-trace formulation, not the kernel dictionary,
carries the gain; the dictionary contributes 0 to 8%
(@sec-drivaerml-trace-factorial). On the DrivAerML interior task the
exact-kernel decoder is 8.0x behind GeoTransolver-volume (pressure
relative L2 0.496 against 0.062, both at 10,000 surface and 10,000
interior points), and its apparently good far-field pressure is a
zero-output artefact (@sec-interior). That comparison is not
resource-matched: GeoTransolver-volume has 9.0M parameters, MT1's
parameter count on the interior task was not recorded, and the two were
not held to a common training memory. What survives at industrial scale
is the contract side: exact equivariance and query independence, and
robustness to biased sampling density. Under a 10:1 density bias on
DrivAerML, MT1 degrades about 1.8x (1.6–2.2x over three seeds), against
GeoTransolver's 3.6x and 13–14.5x for MT2 in the constant-gauge
configuration behind every MT2 accuracy figure in this book; only MT2 with
the similarity gauge on, which is not that configuration, does better at
1.20x (@sec-limits collects the scope statements).

### Relation to MeshTransformer2

MeshTransformer2 (MT2, @sec-mt2) inverts this chapter's central trade.
It keeps exact rotation and translation covariance, enforced once at the
network's edges by reducing every point to invariants and expanding
vector outputs in an equivariant basis, and it keeps global routing, now
through soft-slice attention with equivariant anchors rather than signed
moments. It drops the kernel dictionary, whose potential-flow prior fails
on the separated flows MT2 targets, and with it the linearity and
superposition contracts and the per-layer typed scalar/vector streams. It
also gives up MT1's query independence in its reference configuration:
MT2's heads read from interacting encoder tokens, so a prediction at one
point depends weakly on which other points are in the sample; the optional
`query_independent` configuration with passive read blocks (11.0M
parameters) is exactly query-independent and costs 3.0x to 3.7x in
accuracy on DrivAerML. In exchange the reference configuration spends
its interior on the empirically strongest routing at 8.9M parameters, and
its accuracy on industrial data is the subject of Part II. MT1 remains the architecture of record for the controlled
suites, where a known operator makes an exact prior a contract rather
than a gamble.
